title: Madhuri Dixit Turns 59 With a Dead Body: 'Maa Behen' Hits Netflix Globally on June 4
excerpt: The Dhak Dhak queen teams up with Triptii Dimri in Suresh Triveni's crime-comedy about a mother-daughter trio hiding a corpse — and it drops worldwide on her birthday
body:
There are birthday gifts, and then there's Madhuri Dixit getting a worldwide Netflix premiere on the day she turns 59.

Maa Behen, the crime-comedy that pairs Madhuri with Triptii Dimri and newcomer Dharna Durgaa, arrives on Netflix on June 4 — a global simultaneous release that means NRI audiences from New Jersey to Newham won't have to dodge spoilers or wait for "international dates." It streams everywhere, all at once. Mark your calendars.

The Setup

Directed by Suresh Triveni — the man behind Tumhari Sulu and the critically acclaimed Jalsa — Maa Behen follows a dysfunctional mother and her two daughters who discover a dead body and proceed to make every wrong decision imaginable. The teaser promises a cocktail of dark humour, family drama, and escalating chaos as the trio tries to hide the corpse while their own secrets start unravelling.

Think Drishyam if it were directed by someone who'd grown up on Fargo. Or, as Netflix India's tagline puts it: "a rooted crime-comedy packed with chaos, comedy, and full-blown kaand."

Why This Cast Works

Madhuri Dixit has been on a quiet renaissance. After years of judging dance reality shows, her Netflix series The Fame Game proved she could carry long-form streaming content with the same grace she brings to a Garba sequence. In Maa Behen, she plays the matriarch — a woman who's clearly been keeping her own secrets long before the dead body shows up.

Opposite her, Triptii Dimri is the moment. Fresh off Animal and Bad Newz, she's become Gen Z's Bollywood favourite, equally comfortable in art-house and commercial chaos. The generational pairing — Madhuri's 90s elegance against Triptii's feral millennial energy — is the kind of casting that makes a film feel inevitable.

Rounding out the cast is Dharna Durgaa as the third family member, and Ravi Kishan, who presumably plays the kind of character Ravi Kishan always plays: someone you underestimate at your peril.

The Suresh Triveni Factor

For those tracking careers rather than just movies, Suresh Triveni is becoming one of Hindi cinema's most interesting directors. Tumhari Sulu was a warm comedy about a housewife becoming an overnight radio star. Jalsa was a moral thriller about hit-and-run guilt. Maa Behen appears to split the difference — finding humour in moral crisis, and crisis in family dynamics.

His films share a common thread: ordinary women in extraordinary situations, making choices that are both relatable and deeply questionable. Madhuri Dixit hiding a dead body is, in a way, the logical endpoint of this trajectory.

The NRI Angle

Here's what matters for diaspora audiences: June 4 is a global drop. No theatrical window to wait out. No region-locked delays. You can watch Maa Behen on the same Netflix account you use for Squid Game and Wednesday, from your couch in Chicago or your living room in London.

This is increasingly how Bollywood reaches NRI audiences — not through overpriced PVR screenings at the local multiplex, but through simultaneous streaming drops that treat international viewers as first-class citizens. Netflix India has been especially aggressive about this, and Maa Behen is the latest example.

For desi families abroad, the premise alone — a mother and daughters trying to cover up a disaster while bickering about whose fault it is — will feel uncomfortably familiar. Minus the dead body, hopefully.

The Bottom Line

Maa Behen drops June 4 on Netflix worldwide. Set your reminders. Tell your WhatsApp group. And if your mum asks why you're watching a movie about hiding a dead body, just tell her Madhuri Dixit is in it. That usually works.
